questions.q: Why do STIX/TAXII, CSV, and JSON threat feeds each need their own normalization function in this lesson's approach?
options: Because each feed format represents the same indicator in a different shape, and converting everything into one shared schema keeps downstream lookup/scoring/detection code from needing to understand every format
Because TAXII feeds cannot contain IP addresses, only file hashes
Because Python's requests library cannot parse JSON responses
Because STIX patterns are always written in valid Python syntax and can be eval()'d directly
questions.explain: A normalization layer isolates each feed format's quirks in one function, so everything downstream only ever deals with one common NormalizedIOC shape.

questions.q: In the TAXII pull example, what does `TAXIICollectionSource` combined with `source.query([Filter("type", "=", "indicator")])` actually return?
options: A raw CSV string that still needs to be parsed with csv.DictReader
A pandas DataFrame indexed by IOC value
A list of STIX Indicator objects, each with fields like .pattern, .confidence, and .valid_from
A single boolean indicating whether the feed is reachable
questions.explain: Querying a TAXIICollectionSource for objects of type "indicator" returns STIX Indicator objects; the pattern string (e.g. ipv4-addr:value) still has to be parsed out to extract the actual observable.

questions.q: What does `resp.raise_for_status()` protect against when pulling a CSV/JSON feed with requests?
options: It prevents the script from exceeding Python's recursion limit
It automatically retries the request up to three times
It encrypts the HTTP request before sending it
It turns a failed HTTP response (like a 500 error page) into an exception instead of letting that error page get silently parsed as if it were real threat data
questions.explain: Without raise_for_status(), a 4xx/5xx response's body (often an HTML error page) would flow straight into csv.DictReader or json parsing as if it were legitimate feed content.

questions.q: In the dedupe() function shown in this lesson, what key is used to identify the "same" IOC across multiple feeds, and what happens when a duplicate is found?
options: Keyed on source feed name alone; the first feed pulled always wins regardless of confidence
Keyed on (ioc_type, value.lower()); whichever copy has the higher confidence score is kept
Keyed on first_seen timestamp; the oldest record always wins
Keyed on a random UUID generated per pull, so no two IOCs are ever considered duplicates
questions.explain: dedupe() keys on the (ioc_type, value) pair and keeps whichever copy has the higher confidence, so an IOC multiple feeds agree on survives with its strongest score.

questions.q: Why does this lesson normalize feeds into a NormalizedIOC dataclass instead of just passing around each feed's raw dict/object?
options: A dataclass is required for Python to make HTTP requests
Raw STIX objects cannot be stored in a Python list
Dataclasses automatically deduplicate IOCs without any extra code
A single shared type means every later step — SIEM lookups, scoring, writing back into detection rules — only has to know one schema instead of one per feed source
questions.explain: The whole point of normalization is that everything downstream in the chapter only ever imports and works with NormalizedIOC, regardless of which feed format the data originally came from.
